strengths: Locals framed as impatient people who still stay in line—face of patience ≠ inner calm, complaints later to friends
Teachers framed as safety/throughput (‘if you push, someone gets hurt’), not ‘because we are Japanese’
meiwaku, number-ticket hovering as local cutting, konbini microwave order, and staff tapping someone back two meters are everyday, not tourist-brochure
Staff teaching the line in real time matches how the habit is actually maintained

issues.location: How Japanese People Experience Waiting — meiwaku gloss
issues.problem: meiwaku is narrowed to ‘trouble for people behind you.’ Locals use it more broadly (blocking a path, noise, making staff do extra work).
issues.suggestion: Keep the queue example; gloss meiwaku as imposing trouble on others, then specify the line.

issues.location: Order You Can See / school rehearsal
issues.problem: The everyday local name for platform lining (seiretsu jōsha / 整列乗車) never appears, so a term commuters actually see on posters is missing.
issues.suggestion: Introduce **seiretsu jōsha (整列乗車)** once, with a short gloss, without turning the piece into a vocabulary lesson.

issues.problem: Tying queuing to students cleaning classrooms is editorial sibling-glue more than a local association. Adults lining up at a bakery are not thinking of sōji.
issues.suggestion: Keep school lining and drills; drop or soften the cleaning-classroom parallel.

issues.location: ‘poetry of queuing’ / ‘public movement has a correct shape’
issues.problem: Slightly puts essay psychology in local heads. Many people just follow the paint.
issues.suggestion: Prefer ‘they are not romantic about waiting’ / ‘they expect movement to have a usual pattern.’
